newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU no-win referee in grain exporter bidding.
newsitem.headline: EU no-win referee in grain exporter bidding.

text.p: The European Union risked being snared in a cut-throat battle between grain exporters over subsidies on Thursday as traders scrambled to secure export refunds for wheat at the weekly tender, grain traders said.

Grain exporters which usually wrestle with Brussels over the value of subsidies needed to match lower world prices are now at each others' throats for control of export licences already in the market -- and some face mounting losses, the traders said.

Tension is rife between a handful of exporters believed to be long of subsidised licences and others increasingly desperate to secure subsidies even though they may not be large enough to cover prices at which they sold European wheat in recent months.
"There's no doubt about it, there's a squeeze on in that market," a British trader said as the level of subsidy sought at the weekly auction slid sharply on Thursday.

Whereas the EU's executive Commission awarded subsidies up to 12.90 Ecus per tonne at the previous tender, exporters showed on Thursday they were prepared to accept refunds in single digits to avoid plunging further into loss, dealers said.

And in a manoeuvre that heightened talk of a deliberate squeeze, one firm increased the stakes further by asking for just 6.77 Ecus -- a move that could further weaken the position of those trying to secure far higher refunds, traders said.
"He is trying to take the place of the Commission. He is forcing everyone to come to him," said one trader about the firm that put in the lowest refund bid, valid for 100,000 tonnes.
The company's name was not officially disclosed but traders guessed it was not one of those that had been caught short.
Some are reported to need Ecu refunds in the high teens to avoid making losses on previous sales in the low $140s per tonne, compared with current prices about $15 per tonne higher.
Now, the Commission faces a tough dilemma about where to put the maximum refund level this week, traders said.

If it issues too many licences by pegging the refund too high, it will reduce the losses of firms that had previously tried to gamble against it by selling at low world prices in the belief refunds would rise.
It could also threaten the EU's objective of maintaining discipline in internal prices, which have been rising fast.
If the Commission swallows just a few bids or none at all, it may risk accentuating the squeeze on export licences.
That squeeze tightened sharply earlier this week when export refunds changed hands between exporters at eight Ecus per tonne, or nearly five Ecus less than last week's maximum award.
The buyer refunds the difference between the licence value and the traded value, implying a loss in the current market.
The Commission gave a strong signal it was unhappy about the market fracas on Wednesday when it slashed its wheat flour refund by 40 percent to 10 Ecus per tonne.
An EU official said this was done to "prevent speculation" caused by too wide a gap between flour and grain refunds.

Traders said a fairly neutral response would be to keep the volume of wheat exports at Thursday's tender unchanged at around 400,000 tonnes. This would imply a maximum refund around 10 Ecus and would cover some of the market shorts -- who mostly bid nine to 10 Ecus -- though probably with some financial loss to them.
-- Tim Hepher, Paule Bonjean, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
